hypothesis.title: Adaptive Reward Model Pessimism for Inference-Time Alignment
hypothesis.summary: This paper proposes an adaptive pessimism mechanism for reward models during inference-time alignment, dynamically adjusting reward scores based on uncertainty estimates to mitigate overoptimization. The method combines reward model predictions with confidence intervals derived from model calibration, penalizing high-reward outputs with low confidence. Evaluated on Best-of-N sampling tasks, it demonstrates reduced reward hacking and improved alignment with true human preferences compared to static reward models. Experiments use the Anthropic HH-RLHF dataset and measure success via human evaluation and reward model robustness.
hypothesis.gap: Existing reward models for inference-time alignment treat reward scores as absolute, ignoring uncertainty, which leads to overoptimization when the reward model is imperfect. Current methods like Best-of-N or MBR-BoN do not adaptively adjust for reward model confidence.
hypothesis.approach: Introduce a calibrated pessimism layer that adjusts reward scores by subtracting a penalty proportional to the reward model's uncertainty. The penalty is derived from the model's calibration error on a held-out validation set, ensuring conservative scoring for low-confidence predictions. This adjusted reward is used in Best-of-N sampling.
hypothesis.evaluation: Baselines include vanilla Best-of-N, MBR-BoN, and InferenceTimePessimism. Metrics are reward hacking rate (measured by divergence from human-labeled preferences), alignment score (human evaluation), and reward model calibration error. The Anthropic HH-RLHF dataset is used for training and evaluation.

refined.title: Adaptive Calibration Penalty for Reward Model Uncertainty in Inference-Time Alignment
refined.summary: This paper introduces an adaptive calibration penalty that adjusts reward scores during inference-time alignment by penalizing high-reward outputs with low confidence. The penalty is derived from the reward model's calibration error on a held-out validation set, ensuring conservative scoring for uncertain predictions. Evaluated on Best-of-N sampling tasks, the method reduces reward hacking and improves alignment with true preferences compared to static reward models. Experiments use the Anthropic HH-RLHF dataset and measure success via human evaluation, reward model robustness, and ablation studies isolating the penalty's impact.
refined.gap: Current inference-time alignment methods like Best-of-N (ref-003) and MBR-BoN (ref-003) treat reward scores as absolute, ignoring uncertainty. While ref-004's InferenceTimePessimism and ref-012's LARA address uncertainty, they use rejection sampling or constrained optimization, not direct reward score adjustment based on calibration error. No method penalizes reward scores proportionally to the reward model's uncertainty as measured by calibration error.
refined.approach: The adaptive calibration penalty modifies reward scores by subtracting a penalty term proportional to the reward model's calibration error on a held-out validation set. The penalty is computed as the absolute difference between the model's predicted reward and the empirical reward quantile for the predicted confidence bin. This adjusted reward is used in Best-of-N sampling. Inputs: reward model, validation set, confidence bins. Outputs: penalized reward scores. Objective: minimize penalized reward while maximizing true alignment. The penalty term is the only change from vanilla Best-of-N.
refined.evaluation: Baselines include vanilla Best-of-N (ref-003), MBR-BoN (ref-003), InferenceTimePessimism (ref-004), and LARA (ref-012). Metrics are reward hacking rate (fraction of high-reward outputs rejected by human evaluators), alignment score (human preference win rate), and reward model calibration error (Brier score). The Anthropic HH-RLHF dataset is used. Ablation studies vary the penalty magnitude and calibration bin size to isolate the penalty's effect.

hypothesis.title: Inference-Time Pessimism with Safety Constraints for Scalable LLM Alignment
hypothesis.summary: This paper proposes integrating inference-time pessimism with safety constraints to improve LLM alignment. By combining rejection sampling with dynamic safety thresholds, the method adaptively allocates test-time compute to balance response quality and safety. The approach is validated on benchmarks like HarmBench and JailbreakBench, comparing it to BoN and LARA using metrics like attack success rate and harmlessness scores.
hypothesis.gap: Existing inference-time alignment methods (e.g., BoN, LARA) either degrade with large N or lack formal safety guarantees, leaving a gap in scalable, safety-aware alignment.
hypothesis.approach: Propose a hybrid method combining InferenceTimePessimism's rejection sampling with LARA's Lagrangian constraints. The algorithm dynamically adjusts safety thresholds during sampling, rejecting responses that violate safety constraints while optimizing for quality. A dual variable calibrates the tradeoff between helpfulness and harmlessness.
hypothesis.evaluation: Evaluate on HarmBench and JailbreakBench against baselines (BoN, LARA, ShieldGemma) using attack success rate (ASR), harmlessness scores, and helpfulness metrics. Measure compute efficiency via FLOPs-to-performance curves.

This directly contradicts the hypothesis's assertion that LARA lacks formal safety guarantees. refined.title: Inference-Time Pessimism with Dynamic Safety Thresholds for Scalable LLM Alignment
refined.summary: This paper proposes integrating InferenceTimePessimism's rejection sampling with dynamic safety thresholds derived from LARA's dual calibration. The method adaptively allocates test-time compute to balance response quality and safety by rejecting responses violating safety constraints while optimizing for helpfulness. Evaluated on HarmBench and JailbreakBench, the approach is compared to BoN, LARA, and ShieldGemma using attack success rate, harmlessness, and helpfulness metrics, with an ablation isolating the effect of dynamic thresholds.
refined.gap: While LARA (ref-012) provides formal safety guarantees through Lagrangian constraints, it does not address compute scaling with N. InferenceTimePessimism (ref-004) scales safely with N but lacks explicit safety constraints. No method combines both to adaptively balance quality and safety under compute constraints.
refined.approach: The method combines InferenceTimePessimism's rejection sampling with LARA's dual-calibrated safety constraints. Inputs: a prompt, a pre-trained LLM, a reward model, a cost model, and a compute budget (N). Output: a response. The algorithm: (1) samples N responses, (2) uses the cost model to score each for safety, (3) applies a dynamic safety threshold (α) derived from LARA's dual variable, (4) rejects responses exceeding the cost threshold, (5) re-ranks the remaining using the reward model, (6) returns the top response. The core difference from LARA is the addition of rejection sampling with a dynamic α, and from InferenceTimePessimism is the use of a cost model for safety constraints. The dynamic α is computed as the (1-1/N) quantile of the cost model's scores on a calibration set, ensuring at least one response passes the threshold as N increases.
refined.evaluation: Evaluate on HarmBench (ref-014) and JailbreakBench (ref-017) against baselines: BoN (ref-003), LARA (ref-012), and ShieldGemma (ref-005). Metrics: attack success rate (ASR), harmlessness score (0-100), and helpfulness score (0-100). Compute efficiency: FLOPs per response vs. harmlessness score. Ablation: compare dynamic α (quantile-based) vs. fixed α (0.5) on the same task, measuring the change in ASR and harmlessness. The evaluation tests the central claim that dynamic safety thresholds improve the safety-quality tradeoff under compute constraints.

By dynamically penalizing high-reward responses that deviate from a reference policy, we maintain alignment with true human preferences. The approach is validated on the Anthropic HH-RLHF and AlpacaFarm datasets, comparing against static reward models and InferenceTimePessimism, with metrics including human preference scores, reward model score variance, and safety evaluations.
hypothesis.gap: Current methods like InferenceTimePessimism (ref-004) and MBR-BoN (ref-003) do not adaptively adjust pessimism based on the difficulty of the prompt or the confidence of the reward model, leading to suboptimal performance when scaling N.
hypothesis.approach: We introduce a dynamic penalty term that scales with the reward model's uncertainty (estimated via ensemble variance) and the prompt's complexity (measured by reference policy entropy). This penalty is applied during Best-of-N reranking, with the strength adjusted per-prompt to balance reward maximization and proximity to the reference distribution.
hypothesis.evaluation: Baselines include standard BoN, MBR-BoN, and InferenceTimePessimism. Metrics are: (1) human preference win rates, (2) reward model score variance across N samples, (3) safety scores on ShieldGemma (ref-005) benchmarks, and (4) compute efficiency (samples per successful alignment).

refined.title: Adaptive Reward Model Pessimism for Scaling-Monotonic Inference-Time Alignment
refined.summary: We propose a method to adaptively adjust reward model pessimism during Best-of-N (BoN) sampling, ensuring that increased test-time compute does not degrade response quality due to reward hacking. The approach dynamically penalizes high-reward responses that deviate from a reference policy, with penalty strength determined by reward model uncertainty (ensemble variance) and prompt complexity (reference policy entropy). The method is evaluated on the Anthropic HH-RLHF and AlpacaFarm datasets, comparing against BoN, MBR-BoN, and InferenceTimePessimism, with metrics including human preference win rates, reward model score variance, and safety scores.
refined.gap: InferenceTimePessimism (ref-004) and MBR-BoN (ref-003) do not explicitly adapt penalty strength to both reward model uncertainty and prompt complexity. InferenceTimePessimism uses fixed rejection sampling thresholds, and MBR-BoN applies a static proximity regularization term, leaving open the question of how to dynamically balance reward maximization and reference policy alignment as N scales.
refined.approach: The method introduces a dynamic penalty term: P = α * (1 - R) + β * H, where R is the reward model score, H is the reference policy entropy of the prompt, and α, β are hyperparameters. The penalty is applied during BoN reranking, with α scaled by the ensemble variance of the reward model. The reference policy entropy H is computed as the Shannon entropy of a pre-trained model's output logits for the prompt. The approach differs from InferenceTimePessimism (ref-004) by using a continuous penalty rather than binary rejection and from MBR-BoN (ref-003) by incorporating reward model uncertainty into the penalty strength.
refined.evaluation: Baselines include BoN, MBR-BoN, and InferenceTimePessimism. Metrics are: (1) human preference win rates (evaluated on 1,000 samples from HH-RLHF and AlpacaFarm), (2) reward model score variance across 1,000 BoN samples (to measure reward hacking), (3) safety scores using ShieldGemma (ref-005) (binary classification of harmful content), and (4) compute efficiency (alignment success rate per sample, measured as the number of samples required to achieve 80% human preference win rate). Ablations include: (a) fixed penalty strength, (b) penalty without reward model uncertainty, and (c) penalty without prompt complexity.

hypothesis.title: Inference-Time Pessimism for Reward-Hacking Resilience in Best-of-N Sampling
hypothesis.summary: We propose Inference-Time Pessimism (ITP), a method that introduces a rejection threshold during Best-of-N (BoN) sampling to prevent reward hacking. ITP adaptively discards low-quality samples using a calibrated pessimism score derived from a reward model's uncertainty. This approach is validated on the Anthropic HH-RLHF and AlpacaFarm datasets, comparing ITP-BoN against standard BoN and MBR-BoN. Metrics include reward model score, human preference alignment, and safety ratings, with ITP expected to show reduced reward hacking and improved generalization under high N.
hypothesis.gap: Current BoN methods suffer from reward hacking when N is large, as they over-optimize imperfect reward models without accounting for their uncertainty. Existing solutions like MBR-BoN do not fully address the compute-scaling tradeoff or provide formal guarantees against degradation.
hypothesis.approach: ITP augments BoN with a pessimism score that penalizes samples based on the reward model's confidence interval. A dynamic threshold, derived from the reward model's calibration on a held-out set, rejects samples with scores below the lower bound of the interval. This ensures that only samples with high-probability alignment to the true reward are selected, even as N increases.
hypothesis.evaluation: Baselines include standard BoN, MBR-BoN, and InferenceTimePessimism (ref-004). Metrics are reward model score, human preference (from ref-003), and safety ratings (ref-005). We test on the HH-RLHF and AlpacaFarm datasets, measuring performance as N scales from 10 to 10,000. ITP is expected to maintain or improve performance with increasing N, unlike BoN, which degrades due to reward hacking.
